title: How drugs work: a key in a lock
blurb: Zoom into proteins and watch real drugs sitting in their pockets.

text.simple: Proteins are tiny machines with a shape. Many drugs work by plugging a hole in the machine so it can't work. The yellow sticks are a drug called **imatinib**.
text.student: This is the ABL kinase (the working part of BCR-ABL1) with **imatinib** in its ATP pocket. With the pocket plugged, the kinase can't pass on growth signals. [@druker2001]
text.deep: Imatinib binds the inactive 'DFG-out' conformation of the ABL kinase domain, occupying the ATP site and an adjacent hydrophobic pocket, which underlies its relative selectivity. [@pdb]

text.simple: A drug has to fit its pocket really well, like a key in a lock. This is palbociclib inside CDK6, a protein that pushes cells to divide.
text.student: Drug designers use 3D structures like this one to tweak a molecule until it fits tightly (**potency**) and fits *only* this lock (**selectivity**).
text.deep: Structure-based design optimizes complementary shape, hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts; selectivity across ~500 human kinases is a central challenge for ATP-site inhibitors.

text.simple: Some drugs block a protein that's holding a brake down. Nutlin-3a fills the groove MDM2 uses to grab p53, so p53 is set free.
text.student: MDM2 normally binds and destroys p53. Nutlin-3a occupies the p53-binding groove (shown), releasing p53, but only helps if the cell's p53 is still working. [@vassilev2004]
text.deep: Nutlins mimic three key p53 residues (Phe19, Trp23, Leu26) that insert into MDM2's hydrophobic cleft; efficacy requires wild-type TP53. [@vassilev2004]

quiz.q: What do the yellow sticks in the 3D views show?
quiz.explain: Ribbons are protein; yellow sticks are the drug or small molecules bound to it.

q.simple: What does it mean for a drug to be 'selective'?
q.student: What does 'selectivity' mean in drug design?

options: It acts on its target and not on many other proteins
quiz.explain: Selective drugs fit one 'lock' well and others poorly, which helps reduce side effects.

quiz.q: Why would nutlin-3a do little in K562 cells?
quiz.explain: Freeing p53 only helps if p53 works; K562's TP53 is inactivated. [@law1993]
